93:
In passages such as 'Sutta, Geyya,' etc. (Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.73), it occurs in the sense of the scriptures to be learned (pariyatti). In passages such as 'At that time, there are phenomena (dhammā), there are aggregates (khandhā)' (Dhammasaṅgaṇī 121), it occurs in the sense of non-substantiality (nissatta). But here, it occurs in the sense of qualities (guṇa). Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as: 'Monks, there are other qualities of the Tathāgata (other than the aforementioned virtues).'

'Gambhīra' (deep) means that, just as the great ocean cannot be fathomed by a needle made of a mosquito's proboscis, these qualities cannot be fathomed by the knowledge of anyone other than the Tathāgata. Because they are deep, they are 'duddasa' (hard to see). Because they are hard to see, they are 'duranubodha' (hard to understand). They are 'santa' (peaceful) because all the fevers of defilements have been extinguished; they are also peaceful because they occur in peaceful objects. They are 'paṇīta' (sublime) in the sense of being insatiable, like delicious food. Because they are the domain of supreme knowledge, they cannot be reached by reasoning; thus they are called 'atakkāvacara' (beyond the sphere of logic). Because they are subtle and fine in nature, they are called 'nipuṇa' (subtle). Because they are not the domain of the foolish but can be known only by the wise, they are called 'paṇḍitavedanīya' (to be experienced by the wise).

'Those dhammas which the Tathāgata, having realized by his own higher knowledge, makes known' means: those qualities which the Tathāgata, without being led by others, has personally realized through his own distinguished knowledge and makes known, points out, teaches, and explains. 'Yehi' refers to those qualities. 'Yathābhuccaṃ' means according to reality (as they truly exist). 'Those who would speak rightly in praise [of the Tathāgata] would speak [of them]' means those who wish to speak of the Tathāgata's qualities would be able to speak of them correctly, without omission. What are those dhammas thus praised by the Blessed One? They are indeed the Knowledge of Omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa). If that is so, why is it expressed in the plural (dhammā)? It is because of its association with many consciousnesses and because it has many objects. That Omniscience is found in the four types of functional (kiriya) great consciousness associated with knowledge. For that Omniscience, there is no dhamma that is not its object. As the General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta, taught (in the Paṭisambhidāmagga 1.120): 'Because he knows everything past, it is Omniscience; because there is no obstruction therein, it is Unobstructed Knowledge (anāvaraṇañāṇa),' and so on. Thus, the plural expression is used because of its association with many consciousnesses and because it has many objects through repeated occurrences.

In the word 'aññeva', the particle 'eva' is a word of delimitation (vavatthāpana). It should be applied to all terms thus: 'Only other [qualities], not the virtues such as refraining from taking life,' and 'Only deep, not shallow.' The knowledge of a disciple's perfection (sāvakapāramī-ñāṇa) is deep; the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha (paccekabodhi-ñāṇa) is deeper than that—there is no delimitation there; and the Knowledge of Omniscience is even deeper than that—there is no delimitation there either. But there is nothing deeper than this Omniscience; therefore, the delimitation 'only deep' is applicable. Likewise, it should be understood for all terms, such as 'only hard to see' and 'only hard to understand.'
94:
## Commentary on the Speculators on the Past

"Bhikkhus, what are those teachings?"—this statement is a question asked from the desire to teach those dhammas. "Bhikkhus, there are some recluses and brahmins..." and so on is the answer to the question. If it is asked, "Why is this [detailed analysis of wrong views] undertaken in this way?" The answer is: When the Buddhas reach four subjects, their roar [of teaching] is great, their knowledge penetrates [the taught dhammas] in sequence, the greatness of Buddha-knowledge becomes apparent, the teaching is profound, marked by the three characteristics, and connected with emptiness (suññatā), being devoid of self and what belongs to self.

What are those four? They are: the disciplinary regulations (Vinayapaññatti), the different planes (Bhūmantara), the mode of conditions (Paccayakāra), and the different doctrines (Samayantara). Therefore, regarding the prescription of training rules when a case has arisen, such as: "This training rule is light, this is heavy; this offense is curable, this is incurable; this is an offense, this is not an offense; this leads to falling away [from the Sasana], this leads to rehabilitation, this leads to purification through confession; this is a worldly fault, this is a fault by regulation; in this matter, this training rule should be prescribed"—in such matters of prescribing training rules, others have no strength or power. This is not the domain of others; it is the domain of the Tathāgata alone. Thus, when reaching the disciplinary regulations, the roar of the Buddhas is great, their knowledge penetrates... (omitted) ...connected with emptiness.

Similarly, regarding the four foundations of mindfulness... (omitted) ...the noble eightfold path, the five aggregates, the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, the four noble truths, the twenty-two faculties, the nine roots, the four nutriments, the seven contacts, the seven feelings, the seven perceptions, the seven volitions, the seven consciousnesses. Among these, so many are dhammas of the sense sphere, so many are dhammas included in the fine-material and immaterial spheres, so many are mundane dhammas, and so many are supramundane dhammas—to analyze and teach the Abhidhamma Piṭaka with its twenty-four universal Patthānas and infinite methods, others have no strength or power. This is not the domain of others; it is the domain of the Tathāgata alone. Thus, when reaching the distinction of the different planes, the roar of the Buddhas is great, their knowledge penetrates... (omitted) ...connected with emptiness.

Similarly, this ignorance (avijjā) assists formations (saṅkhāra) by way of nine modes: by being an arising (uppāda), by being an occurrence (pavatta), as a sign (nimitta), as an accumulation (āyūhana), as a conjunction (saṃyoga), as an impediment (palibodha), as an origination (samudaya), as a cause (hetu), and as a condition (paccaya). Likewise, [the Buddha] taught how formations and so on assist consciousness and so on. In accordance with that teaching: "How is the wisdom that encompasses conditions called the knowledge of the stability of Dhamma (dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa)? Ignorance is the stability of arising (uppādaṭṭhiti) and the stability of occurrence (pavattaṭṭhiti) of formations..."
95:
...stability as a sign (nimitta), stability as an accumulation (āyūhana), stability as a conjunction (saṃyoga), stability as an impediment (palibodha), stability as an origination (samudaya), stability as a cause (hetu), and stability as a condition (paccaya). Through these nine modes, ignorance is the condition, formations are conditionally arisen; both these dhammas are conditionally arisen—thus, the wisdom that encompasses conditions is the knowledge of the stability of Dhamma. In the past and in the future, ignorance is the stability of arising... (omitted) ...birth is the stability of arising of aging and death... (omitted) ...is the stability of condition. Through these nine modes, birth is the condition, aging and death are conditionally arisen; both these dhammas are conditionally arisen—thus, the wisdom that encompasses conditions is the knowledge of the stability of Dhamma (Paṭisambhidāmagga 1.45). Thus, to analyze and teach this Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda) which occurs by way of various conditions for various dhammas, with its three rounds, three periods, three links, four summaries, and twenty modes, others have no strength or power. This is not the domain of others; it is the domain of the Buddha alone. Thus, when reaching the mode of conditions, the roar of the Buddhas is great, their knowledge penetrates... (omitted) ...connected with emptiness.

Similarly, there are four types of Eternalism (Sassatavāda), four types of Partial-Eternalism (Ekaccasassatavāda), four types of Extensionism (Antānantika), four types of Eel-wriggling (Amarāvikkhepika), two types of Fortuitous Origination (Adhiccasamuppannika), sixteen types of Percipient Immortality (Saññīvāda), eight types of Non-percipient Immortality (Asaññīvāda), eight types of Neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient Immortality (Nevasaññīnāsaññīvāda), seven types of Annihilationism (Ucchedavāda), and five types of Nibbāna in this life (Diṭṭhadhammanibbānavāda). To analyze these sixty-two views, showing how they take up this [view] based on that [Dependent Origination], and to teach them making them free from tangles and obstructions—others have no strength or power. This is not the domain of others; it is the domain of the Buddha alone. Thus, when reaching the different doctrines, the roar of the Buddhas is great, their knowledge penetrates, the greatness of Buddha-knowledge becomes apparent, the teaching is profound, marked by the three characteristics, and connected with emptiness.

In this context, the different doctrines are found. Therefore, to show the greatness of the knowledge of omniscience and to clarify the manifestation of emptiness in the teaching, the King of Dhamma, the Buddha, having penetrated the different doctrines with his knowledge, undertook the answer to the question: "Bhikkhus, there are some recluses and brahmins."

In that passage, "santi" means they exist, they are found, they are obtained. "Bhikkhave" is a word of address. "Eke" means some people. "Samaṇabrāhmaṇā" means recluses (samaṇas) because of having entered the homeless life, and brahmins (brāhmaṇas) by birth. Or, they are those recognized by the world as recluses and brahmins. Because they speculate and theorize about the beginning (the past) in various ways, they are called "Speculators on the Past" (Pubbantakappikā).
96: They are called 'Pubbantakappikā' because they speculate on the past portion of the aggregates through craving and views. In this term 'Pubbantakappikā', the word 'anta' is found in the senses of end, interior, limit, vileness, the other side, and portion. Indeed, in passages such as "full of intestines (anta), full of stomach," the word 'anta' means intestine. In "they wander in the world covered by followers, pure within (anto), beautiful without," it means interior. In "the end (anto) of the belt is worn out," and "that (fire) reaches the limit (anta) of green grass, or the limit of a path, or the limit of a rock, or the limit of water," it means limit. In "Monks, this livelihood of seeking alms is the lowest (antamidam) among livelihoods," it means vile. In "this (Nibbāna) is the end (anto) of suffering," it means the other side. The cessation of all conditions (Nibbāna) is called the other side or the extreme end of suffering. In "Friends, self-identity is one part (anto)," it means portion. Here too (in Pubbantakappikā), it means portion. The word 'kappa' is also used in many senses such as life-span, slight reason, and disciplinary rule, as in: "Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One remain for an eon (kappa)," "there is a slight reason (kappo) for lying down," and "a cloth made with a 'kappa-bindu' (prescribed mark) is sewn with one not so made." Here, it should be understood in the sense of craving and views. It has been said: "There are two kinds of 'kappa': the craving-kappa and the view-kappa." Therefore, the meaning here is: those who remain speculating and specifically imagining the past portion of the aggregates by the power of craving and views are 'Pubbantakappikā'. For those who remain speculating on the past portion, because they have views that follow only the past by the power of repeated arising, they are called 'Pubbantānudiṭṭhino'. Such individuals, based on, arriving at, and depending on that past portion, make others also hold wrong views and proclaim many kinds of statements of conviction through eighteen grounds. In that context, 'anekavihitāni' means of many kinds. 'Adhimuttipadāni' means words that express designations. Alternatively, views are called 'adhimutti' because they occur by overwhelming the true meaning and not grasping it according to its nature. 'Adhimuttipada' means words that illuminate views. 'By eighteen grounds (vatthūhi)' means by eighteen causes.
97: ## Explanation of Eternalism (Sassatavāda) Now, wishing to explain those eighteen grounds by which they argue and proclaim with firm attention, the Buddha asked a question in the manner of "Te ca kho bhonto," etc., and then said "Santi, bhikkhave," etc., to show those grounds by dividing them in detail. In that passage, it is called 'vāda' because they speak by means of this view; this is a designation for a wrong view. Because those recluses and brahmins have the view "it is eternal," they are 'Sassatavādā' (Eternalists). In this same way, the meaning of similar terms that follow should be understood. "Sassataṃ attānañca lokañca" means they take one of the five aggregates, such as form, as the self and as the world, and designate that self and world as continuous, undying, permanent, and stable. As the General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta, said: "They designate the self and the world as eternal, saying 'Form is the self and the world and is eternal'..." and so on for all five aggregates: form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. In the terms "ātappamanvāya," etc., energy (vīriya) is called 'ātappa' because it burns away (torments) defilements. That same energy is called 'padhāna' because of exertion, and 'anuyoga' because of repeated application. "Anvāya" means following, arriving at, or depending on this three-fold energy. "Appamāda" refers to not being separated from mindfulness. "Sammā manasikāra" means attending to the meditation subject by proper means (the right way), which in essence refers to wisdom (ñāṇa). The wisdom of one who stands in that attention, through which the knowledge of recollection of past lives is accomplished, is what is intended here as 'manasikāra'. Therefore, the brief meaning here is: "depending on energy, mindfulness, and wisdom." "Tathārūpaṃ" means of such a nature. "Ceto-samādhiṃ" means the concentration of the fourth jhāna mind. "Phusati" means attains or acquires. In the phrase "yathā samāhite citte," it means when the mind is well-placed and well-established by that fourth jhāna concentration. The meaning of terms like "anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ" has already been explained in the Visuddhimagga. "So evamāha" means that recluse or brahmin, being endowed with the power of jhāna and mundane direct knowledge, and being one of wrong view, speaks thus. "Vañjho" means barren or sterile, like a barren animal or a barren palm tree, meaning it is fruitless and does not produce anything. By this word 'vañjha', he denies the productivity of the jhāna, etc., which are taken as the self and the world, to produce form, etc. Because it stands like a mountain peak, it is called 'kūṭaṭṭho'. Because it stands firmly like a gate-pillar, it is 'esikaṭṭhāyiṭṭhito'. The meaning is that it stands like a well-dug gate-pillar which remains motionless. By both these metaphors, he shows the absence of destruction of the world. Some teachers, however, read "īsikaṭṭhāyiṭṭhito" and say it stands like the pith (īsika) inside the muñja grass.
98:
Some teachers say this. In that statement, this is the intended meaning: in the context of saying "this thing arises," that self comes out just like a reed (isikā) coming out from muñja grass, having already existed. And because it remains like the reed staying within the muñja grass, those very beings run on from this life to another life; they go from here to elsewhere—this is the meaning.

"Saṃsaranti" means they wander again and again from one life to another. "Cavanti" means they reach the designation of passing away. Likewise, in the word "upapajjanti" (they are reborn), the same method applies. In the Commentary, however, it is stated that after first saying "the self and the world are eternal," by now saying "those beings run on," etc., this holder of views destroys his own doctrine. The vision of a holder of views is not stable; it shakes like a stake driven into a pile of chaff. Like a madman's basket containing pieces of cake, excrement, cow dung, and so on, in this wrong view, there are both good and bad things.

In the phrase "atthi tveva sassatisamaṃ," "sassati" refers to the great earth, which is perceived as always existing; likewise, Mount Sineru, the moon, and the sun are so perceived. Because of such perception, they regard the self as being equal to the earth, Mount Sineru, the moon, and the sun, and thus say, "It exists eternally."

Now, wishing to show the reason for proving the claim "the self and the world are eternal," he said, "For what reason? I, through effort..." and so on. There, in saying "By this I know this," he shows: "Through this specific attainment (the knowledge of recollecting past lives), I know this directly; I do not speak merely out of faith." The letter 'm' [in the Pali] is inserted for the sake of euphonic junction (sandhi). "Bhikkhus, this is the first ground" means among the four grounds mentioned by the word 'vatthu' (grounds/bases), this is the first ground; the ability to recollect about a hundred thousand births is the first cause.

32-33. In the next two sections, the same method applies. Specifically, this first section is spoken in terms of the ability to recollect many hundreds of thousands of births. The other two are spoken in terms of recollecting ten and forty world cycles of contraction and expansion (saṃvaṭṭavivaṭṭakappa). Indeed, a sectarian of dull wisdom recollects only about a hundred thousand births; one of medium wisdom recollects ten world cycles; one of sharp wisdom recollects forty, but not beyond that.

In the fourth section, one is called a "takkī" because he reasons, or because reasoning exists in him. This is a designation for those who take up views through reasoning and reflection. One is called a "vīmaṃsī" because he is endowed with inquiry. Inquiry (vīmaṃsā) consists of weighing, liking, and accepting. Just as a man tests the water with a stick before entering, so too, one who, after weighing...
99:
...after liking and personally accepting, takes up a view, he should be known as a 'vīmaṃsī' (inquirer). 'Takkapariyāhata' means hammered out by logic, reasoned through various methods. 'Vīmaṃsānucarita' means followed by that aforementioned inquiry. 'Sayam-paṭibhāna' means produced merely by one's own intuition. "He says thus" (evamāha) means he speaks in this way after taking up the eternalist view.

In that section on logicians, there are four types of logicians (takkī): the traditionalist (anussutika), the one who remembers past births (jātissara), the one who has gains (lābhī), and the pure logician (suddhatakkika). Among these four, one who hears such words as "There was once a king named Vessantara" and reasons, "If King Vessantara is indeed the Blessed One, then the self is eternal," and thus takes up a view, is called an anussutika logician. One who remembers two or three births and reasons, "I myself was in such a life in the past, therefore the self is eternal," is called a jātissara logician. One who, because of his possession of sensual pleasures, reasons, "As my self is happy in this life, so it was in the past and so it will be in the future," and thus takes up a view, is called a lābhī logician. One who takes up a view merely by reasoning, "When this is, that is," is called a suddhatakkika logician.

"By one of these reasons" means they proclaim it by one, two, or three of these four grounds. "There is nothing outside this" is a bold lion's roar, meaning there is no other reason for proclaiming the eternalist view outside these four grounds.

"Bhikkhus, the Tathāgata knows this" means, Bhikkhus, the Tathāgata knows these four types of views in various ways. To show the manner of that knowing, he said, "These are the grounds of views (diṭṭhiṭṭhāna)," and so on. There, the views themselves are called 'grounds of views.' Furthermore, the causes of views are also 'grounds of views.' As it is said: "What are the eight grounds of views? The aggregates, ignorance, contact, perception, thought, improper attention, bad friends, and the voice of another (pariatoghosa) are the grounds of views." "The aggregates are the cause, the aggregates are the condition, being a ground of views in the sense of being the basis for arising; thus the aggregates are also a ground of views. Ignorance is the cause... [and so on]... bad friends are the cause. The voice of another is the cause, the voice of another is the condition, being a ground of views in the sense of being the basis for arising; thus the voice of another is also a ground of views," as stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga. "Thus taken" (evaṃgahitā) means what is called a view...
100:
Initially, the bases of views (diမ္တhiမ္တhāna) are taken as "The self and the world are eternal"; this is the meaning of being taken, held, and maintained. It is called 'evamparāmaမ္တha' (the view thus misapprehended) because it is repeatedly touched or grasped with a mind free of doubt, having concluded that "Only this is true, everything else is futile." The bases of views, known as causes, are taken in terms of the object, the occurrence, and the cultivation, in such a way that they give rise to views. They are misapprehended through repeated grasping because of not seeing the danger. Those who hold such views have one of the destinations (gati) among hell, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts. "Evaေ abhisamparāyā" is a synonym for the preceding term, meaning they have such a future world.

The Tathāgata knows that view. The Tathāgata knows not only the wrong view along with its cause and its destination, but he knows all of that, and he knows what is far beyond that: virtue, concentration, and omniscience. Even though he knows such incomparable and distinguished Dhamma, he does not misapprehend it by thinking "I know" through the influence of craving, views, or conceit. For the Tathāgata who does not thus misapprehend, the cooling (nibbuti) of those defilements of misapprehension is known by himself. He shows that, "Monks, the Nibbāna of the Tathāgata is evident."

Now, to show the practice by which the Tathāgata attained that cooling, and wishing to teach the meditation subject by way of those feelings (vedanā) in which the sectarians delight—entering the thicket of views thinking "We shall be happy here, we shall be happy in this"—he said, "the origin of feelings," and so forth. Therein, knowing according to reality means: "With the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of feeling"; thus he sees the arising of the aggregate of feeling in the sense of the arising of conditions. "With the arising of craving, there is the arising of feeling"; "With the arising of kamma, there is the arising of feeling"; "With the arising of contact, there is the arising of feeling"; thus he sees the arising of the aggregate of feeling in the sense of the arising of conditions. Even by seeing the characteristic of birth, he sees the arising of the aggregate of feeling. Thus, knowing the origin of feelings according to reality by way of these five characteristics, he sees the passing away of the aggregate of feeling in the sense of the cessation of conditions, saying "With the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of feeling"; "With the cessation of craving, there is the cessation of feeling."
101:
(He sees the passing away of feeling); "With the cessation of kamma, there is the cessation of feeling," thus he sees the passing away of the aggregate of feeling in the sense of the cessation of conditions. "With the cessation of contact, there is the cessation of feeling," thus he sees the passing away of the aggregate of feeling in the sense of the cessation of conditions. One who sees the characteristic of change also sees the passing away of the aggregate of feeling. Thus, knowing the passing away of feelings according to reality by way of these five characteristics, and;

"The pleasure and joy that arise dependent on a feeling—this is the gratification (assāda) of feeling"; thus knowing the gratification according to reality; "That a feeling is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—this is the danger (ādģnava) of feeling"; thus knowing the danger according to reality; "The removal and abandonment of desire and lust for feeling—this is the escape (nissaraေa) from feeling"; thus knowing the escape according to reality. Monks, because the Tathāgata is free from desire and lust, he is without clinging (upādāna) and is liberated through non-clinging. If there were clinging, one would cling to some state, and because of being clung to, there would be an aggregate in a new existence. Because that new aggregate does not exist, without clinging to any state at all, monks, the Tathāgata is liberated (from saဳsāra).

"Monks, these are those [Dhammas]" refers to the Dhammas I asked about: "Monks, what are those Dhammas that are deep?" "Monks, these are those [Dhammas]—the Tathāgata knows that [view] and he knows what is far beyond that." Thus, these qualities of the knowledge of omniscience that have been pointed out should be understood as deep, hard to see... and to be experienced by the wise. By which qualities neither an ordinary person nor any of the noble disciples such as a stream-enterer is able to speak praise of the Tathāgata according to reality. Indeed, only the Tathāgata, wishing to speak praise correctly according to reality, could do so. Thus, the Buddha, in asking, asked only about the knowledge of omniscience; in concluding, he concluded only with that knowledge of omniscience; but in between, he analyzed the views.

## The Explanation of the First Recitation Section is Finished.

## The Explanation of the Doctrine of Partial-Eternalism

'Ekaccasassatika' refers to those who hold the doctrine of partial-eternalism (Ekaccasassatavāda). They are of two types: those who hold that some beings are eternal (satt ekaccasassatika) and those who hold that some formations are eternal (saဳkhār ekaccasassatika). Both types are included here.

"Yaေ" is merely a particle. "Kadāci" means at some time. "Karahaci" is a synonym for that "kadāci." "Dģghassa addhuno" means of a long time. "Accayena" means...
102:
By passing beyond (atikkamena). 'Saṃvattaṭi' means it is destroyed (vinassati). The word 'yebuyyena' (mostly) is spoken with reference to those beings remaining after excluding those who are reborn in the higher Brahma realms or the formless realms. Because they are produced by the jhana-mind, they are called 'manomaya' (mind-made). Because rapture is their food and nutriment, they are called 'pītibakkha' (feeding on rapture). Because they have only their own radiance, they are called 'sayampabhā' (self-luminous). Because they can travel through the sky, they are called 'antalikkhacarā' (sky-walkers).

They are called 'subhaṭṭhāyino' because they dwell in beautiful gardens, mansions, wish-fulfilling trees, and so forth. Alternatively, they are called 'subhaṭṭhāyino' because they exist possessing beautiful and delightful garments and ornaments. 'Ciraṃ dīghamaddhānaṃ' (for a long and protracted time) means, at the maximum, for eight great aeons.

'Vivaṭṭati' means it stands well (saṇṭhāti). 'Suññaṃ brahmavimānaṃ' (an empty Brahma mansion) means it is empty because beings born there naturally do not yet exist; it means the First Jhana Brahma realm arises. There is no creator or instigator of that mansion. However, as stated in the Visuddhimagga, the jeweled ground arises due to seasonal conditions (utu) which have kamma as their cause. In that First Jhana realm, gardens, wish-fulfilling trees, and so forth arise only in their natural places of arising. Then, for beings, a longing (nikanti) arises for the place where they naturally used to dwell. They develop the first jhana and descend from that (higher realm). Therefore, it is said, 'Atha kho aññataro satto' (Then a certain being), and so forth.

'Āyukkhayā vā puññakkhayā vā' (either by the exhaustion of life-span or by the exhaustion of merit) means: those who, having performed noble meritorious deeds, are reborn in some short-lived deva world, are unable to remain by the power of their own merit and pass away according to the life-span of that deva world; this is called 'āyukkhayā cavanti' (passing away by exhaustion of life-span). Those who, having performed small meritorious deeds, are reborn in a long-lived deva world, are unable to remain for the full life-span and pass away in the interval; this is called 'puññakkhayā cavanti' (passing away by exhaustion of merit). 'Dīghamaddhānaṃ tiṭṭhati' (stands for a long time) means one aeon or half an aeon.

'Anabhirati' (discontent) means the longing for other beings to arrive. The kind of boredom associated with aversion (paṭigha) does not exist in the Brahma world. 'Paritassanā' (agitation) means trembling or shaking. It is of four kinds: tāsatassanā (agitation through fear), taṇhātassanā (agitation through craving), diṭṭhitassanā (agitation through views), and ñāṇatassanā (agitation through knowledge). Among these, 'fear, terror, horripilation, and mental agitation arising on account of birth, aging, sickness, and death' is called tāsatassanā. The longing, 'O, may other beings also come to this state,' is called taṇhātassanā. The phrase 'paritassitavipphanditameva' refers to diṭṭhitassanā. 'They also, having heard the Dhamma teaching of the Tathāgata...'
103:
"...having heard the Dhamma teaching, mostly fall into fear, a sense of urgency, and great terror"—this (from the Aṅguttara Nikāya) is called ñāṇatassanā. In this context (of anabhirati and paritassanā), however, both taṇhātassanā and diṭṭhitassanā are appropriate. In the phrase "brahmavimānaṃ", it is not called "suñña" (empty) here because the being who was first reborn (Mahābrahmā) is present. "Upapajjanti" means they arrive by way of rebirth. "Sahabyataṃ" means companionship or the state of being together.

"Abhibhū" means (thinking), "I am the greatest," because of being able to stand having overcome (other beings). "Anabhibhūto" means one who is not overcome by others. "Aññadatthu" is a particle in the sense of "certainly" or "surely". "Daso" means "one who sees all" by way of vision. "Vasavattī" means "I bring all groups of beings under my control." "Issaro kattā nimmātā" means (thinking), "I am the Lord in the world; I am the Maker and the Creator of the world; the earth, the Himalayas, Mount Sineru, the Cakkavāḷa, the great oceans, the moon, and the sun were created by me." "Seṭṭho sajitā" means (thinking), "I am the best in the world and the Appointer; I am the one who thus distributes and appoints beings, saying: 'You be a khattiya, you a brahmin, a vessa, a sudda, a householder, or a renunciant. At the very least, you be a camel, you be an ox.'" "Vasီ pitā bhူtabhavyānaṃ" means (thinking), "I am the Master (vasī) due to practiced mastery; I am the father of those who have been (bhūta) and those who are to be (bhavya)."

Among those (bhūta and bhavya), the egg-born (aṇḍaja) and womb-born (jalābuja) beings are called "bhavya" (to be) while they are inside the eggshell or the womb; from the time they come outside, they are called "bhūta" (have been). Moisture-born (saṃsedaja) beings are called "bhavya" at the first thought-moment (rebirth-linking consciousness); from the second moment onwards, they are called "bhūta". Spontaneously-born (opapātika) beings should be understood as "bhavya" during their first posture; from the second posture onwards, they are called "bhūta". With the perception that all these beings are his children, he thinks, "I am the father of those who have been and those who are to be."

Now, wishing to establish this through a reason, having made the claim (paṭiññā), "These beings were created by me," he said, "For what reason is that?" and so forth. "Itthattaṃ" means this state, meaning the state of a Brahma. "Iminā mayaṃ" means that whether they pass away or are reborn due to the power of their own kamma, merely through mere imagination, they think, "This Brahma created us," and like a curved peg in a curved hole, they bow down and go to the very feet of that (Great Brahma).

"Vaṇṇavantataro ca" means more beautiful, possessing a fine appearance, and inspiring confidence. "Mahesakkhataro" means having greater fame and glory by way of sovereignty and retinue.
104:
This situation indeed exists. That person, having passed away from that Brahma realm, does not go elsewhere but comes to this human world; it is with reference to such a person that this was said. 'From home' (agārasmā) means from the house. 'Homelessness' (anagāriyaṃ) means the life of a renunciant. Since the work of a household, such as farming and cattle herding, does not exist in that state of a renunciant, it is called homelessness. 'Goes forth' (pabbajati) means he approaches [that state]. 'He does not remember beyond that' (tato paraṃ nānussarati) means he cannot remember beyond that one previous life in which he formerly dwelt; being unable to remember, he stops at that previous life and adopts a [wrong] view.

Regarding the terms 'permanent' (nicco) and so on: because he does not see the rebirth of that Great Brahma, he says he is 'permanent'. Because he does not see his passing away, he says he is 'stable' (dhuvo). Because he is ever-present, he says he is 'eternal' (sassata). Because there is no alteration even by the power of old age, he says he is 'of an unchanging nature' (avipariṇāmadhamma). The remaining words are clear as explained in the first section.

## 45-46. In the second section, they are called 'debauched by pleasure' (khiḍḍāpadosikā) because they perish due to excessive indulgence in play. In the Pali text, it is also written as 'padūsikā', but that reading is not in the Commentary. 'Beyond time' (ativelaṃ) means for an excessively long time. 'Indulging in the nature of laughter, play, and delight' (hassakhiḍḍāratidhammasamāpannā) means they have fully entered into and repeatedly practice delight in sexual amusement and delight in physical and vocal play; the meaning is that they dwell endowed with the aforementioned nature of delight.

'Mindfulness is lost' (sati sammussati) means that mindfulness regarding eating food is lost or forgotten. It is said that those deities, while enjoying the festival of the stars with their great glory and wealth obtained through special merit, do not even know whether they have eaten or not because of the greatness of that prosperity. Then, from the time they miss a single meal onwards, even if they eat and drink continuously, they still pass away; they cannot remain. Why is this? It is because of the strength of the kamma-born heat (kammaja-tejo) and the weakness of the physical body (karaja-kāya). In humans, the kamma-born heat is weak, and the physical body is strong. Because their heat is weak and their physical body is strong, humans can still be supported and remain by means of hot water, rice gruel, and so on, even after seven days have passed. However, the heat of the deities is strong, and their physical body is weak. Those deities cannot remain if they miss even a single mealtime. For example, a lotus or a red lotus placed on a hot stone at midday in summer cannot be restored to its normal state even if sprinkled with a hundred jars of water in the evening; it simply perishes. In the same way, even if they eat and drink continuously afterwards, they still pass away.
105:
They cannot remain. Therefore, the Blessed One said, "With the loss of mindfulness, those deities pass away from that group." Which deities are they? There is no specific investigation in the Commentary stating "these are the deities." However, since it is stated generally without distinction that "the kamma-born heat of deities is strong, and the physical body is weak," it should be understood that whichever deities live depending on solid food (kabaḷīkārāhāra) and indulge in play in this way, they are the ones who pass away. Some teachers, however, say, "Those deities are the Nimmānarati and Paranimmitavasavatti devas." They are called 'debauched by pleasure' (khiḍḍāpadosikā) simply because they perish through excessive play. The rest should be understood in the same manner as the previous method.

47-48. In the third section, they are called 'debauched by mind' (manopadosikā) because they are corrupted or perish by the mind [of ill-will]. These are the deities of the Realm of the Four Great Kings (Cātumahārājika). It is said that among them, one young deva, intending to play at the festival of the stars, sets out on the road in a chariot with his retinue. Then, another young deva, coming out from his mansion and seeing the one going before him, becomes angry, thinking, "Friends, this poor wretch is going as if he has never seen such wealth before, as if he is bursting with joy, or as if he is being broken by joy." The one going in front also turns back and, seeing that the other is angry (since those who are angry are easily recognized), and knowing his state of anger, gets angry in return, saying, "You are angry, but what can you do to me? This prosperity was obtained by me through the power of giving, virtue, and so on, not through your power." If only one is angry and the other is not, he can still be protected from passing away. But when both are angry, the anger of one becomes a condition for the other, and the anger of the other becomes a condition for the first; thus, both pass away even in the midst of their weeping harem. This is the natural law in this case. The rest should be understood in the same manner as already stated.

49-52. In the view of the logician (takkīvāda), this logician sees the breaking up of the eye and so on. However, because the mind (citta) ceases only after giving a condition from the preceding mind to the succeeding mind, he does not see the breaking up of the mind, which is even more powerful [subtle/rapid] than the breaking up of the eye and so on. Not seeing that, he says [that the self is permanent], assuming that just as a bird leaves one tree and perches on another, so too, when this body breaks up, the mind goes elsewhere. The rest should be understood in the same manner as already stated.

## Explanation of the Doctrine of Finitism and Infinitism (Antānantavāda)
'Antānantikā' refers to those who hold the doctrine of finitism and infinitism. The meaning is the doctrines that proceed based on the world being finite, or infinite, or both finite and infinite, or neither finite nor infinite.
106:
54-60. "Dwells perceiving the world as finite" means not expanding the counterpart sign (paṭibhāganimitta) to the limit of the world-system (cakkavāḷa), but taking that very sign as "the world" and dwelling with the perception that the world is finite. However, one who has a kasiṇa that is expanded to the limit of the world-system is one who perceives it as infinite. If one does not expand it upwards or downwards but only horizontally (sideways), one perceives it as finite upwards and downwards, and infinite horizontally. The view of a reasoner (takkīvāda) should be understood in the same way as previously mentioned. All four of these types follow what they have previously seen and, because they hold onto it with wrong view, they are included among the speculators about the past (pubbantakappika).

## Explanation of the Doctrine of Eel-wriggling (Amarāvikkhepavāda-vaṇṇanā)
It is called "amarā" because it does not die (it is interminable). What is this "amarā"? It is the view and the speech of one with wrong view that is without limit, following the method such as "I do not hold it thus," and so on. Various rejections are called "vikkhepa." Rejection through various views and speech that are interminable is called "amarāvikkhepa." Those who have this eel-wriggling are called "amarāvikkhepikā." Another way: there is a species of fish called "amarā" (eel). Just as that fish, by surfacing and diving as it swims in the water, cannot be caught, so too this doctrine runs here and there and does not come to be grasped (as a definite position); thus it is called "amarāvikkhepa." Those who hold this doctrine are called "amarāvikkhepikā."

"He does not know as it really is, 'This is wholesome'" means he does not know the ten wholesome courses of action (kusalakammapatha) as they really are. Regarding the unwholesome, the ten unwholesome courses of action are also intended. "That [not knowing] would be a distress to me" means that because of the arising of remorse (vippaṭisāra) thinking "I have spoken a lie," it would be a distress to me, it would be suffering. "That distress would be an obstacle to me" means that distress would be an obstacle to my reaching heaven (sagga) and the path (magga). "Fear of lying (musāvāda-bhaya) and abhorrence of lying (musāvāda-parijegucchā)" means through fear of wrongdoing (ottappa) and shame (hiri) regarding false speech. "He resorts to evasion of speech (vācāvikkhepa)" means he resorts to various rejections of speech. What kind of rejection? It means the endless rejection called eel-wriggling (amarāvikkhepa).

Among the phrases such as "I do not hold it thus," "I do not hold it thus" is an indefinite evasion. "I do not hold it that way" rejects the eternalist view (sassatavāda) which says, "The self and the world are eternal." "I do not hold it otherwise" rejects the partial-eternalist view (ekaccasassatavāda) which is stated differently from eternalism. "I do not say it is not" means—"Not...
107:
...it rejects annihilationism (ucchedavāda) which says, 'The Tathāgata exists after death.' It rejects the view of a reasoner (takkīvāda) which says, 'He neither exists nor does not exist.' As for himself, when asked 'Is this thing wholesome?' or 'Is it unwholesome?', he does not provide any answer. When asked 'Is this thing wholesome?', he says 'I do not hold it thus.' Then when asked 'Is it unwholesome?', he says 'I do not hold it that way.' When asked 'Is it something other than both?', he says 'I do not hold it as something other.' Then when asked 'If it is not in any of these three ways, what is your view?', he says 'I do not say it is not.' Then when asked 'Is your view that it is not-not?', he says 'I do not say it is not-not.' In this way, he resorts only to evasion (vikkhepa—various rejections) and does not stand on any one side.

"Desire (chanda) or lust (rāga)" means that even if he does not know specifically, he might impulsively say "this is wholesome" to what is wholesome, and "this is unwholesome" to what is unwholesome, and then ask other wise people, "I have answered such a person in this way; is that answer well-spoken?" When those wise people say, "Friend, you have well-spoken; you have answered wholesome as wholesome and unwholesome as unwholesome," he thinks, "There is no wise man equal to me." In this way, desire or lust would arise in him regarding that answer. Here, chanda is weak lust, and rāga is strong lust. "Ill-will (dosa) or resentment (paṭigha)" means that if he says "unwholesome" to what is wholesome, or "wholesome" to what is unwholesome, and asks other wise people, and they say, "You have answered poorly," he thinks, "I do not even know this much." In this way, ill-will or resentment would arise in him regarding that error. Here too, dosa is weak anger, and paṭigha is strong anger.

"That would be a clinging (upādāna) for me; that would be a distress (vighāta) for me" means those two, desire and lust, would be my clinging, and those two, ill-will and resentment, would be distress. Or, both are called clinging by way of firm grasping, and distress (vighāta) by way of afflicting. For lust, because it does not wish to let go, grasps the object like a leech. Ill-will is like a cobra because it wishes to destroy. Both of these are called "clinging" and "distress" because they afflict by way of burning. The rest of the text is similar to the first section.
108:
Paṇḍita refers to those who are endowed with wisdom. Nipuṇa refers to those who possess subtle and refined intellect, capable of penetrating various subtle and profound meanings. Kataparappavāda refers to those who have already understood the doctrines of others and have also practiced engaging in debates with others. Vālavedhirūpa refers to those who are like archers capable of splitting a hair.

Te bhindantā manye means that just as an archer capable of splitting a hair pierces the hair, these individuals also wander about, as if breaking and destroying the subtle views of others with the range of their own wisdom.

Te maṃ tattha means those recluses and brahmins (would question) me regarding those wholesome and unwholesome states. Samanuyuñjeyyuṃ means they would ask about one's doctrine, saying, "What is wholesome? What is unwholesome? State your doctrine." Samanugāheyuṃ means when it is stated, "This is such," they would cross-examine and investigate the reason, saying, "For what reason do you hold this meaning?" Samanubhāseyyuṃ means when it is stated, "I hold it for such a reason," they would point out the fault in that reason and urge or prompt him, saying, "You do not know this; take only this, abandon that."

Na sampāyeyya means he would not be able to complete it; it means he would not be able to speak so as to complete the explanation. So mama-assa vighāto means that the inability to complete the explanation even after speaking repeatedly would be my distress; it means it would only be the physical suffering and exhaustion of the drying of the lips, palate, tongue, and throat. The rest of the arrangement here is just the same as in the first round.

65-66. Manda means one of dull wisdom; this is indeed a name for one without wisdom. Momūha means one who is extremely deluded. In the passages beginning with hoti tathāgato, the term "Tathāgata" is intended as a being (satta). The rest of the meaning here is plain. These four types of individuals are also included among the Pubbantakappikas (Speculators about the Past) because they have grasped views by following the sequence of states that occurred in the past.

## Adhiccasamuppannavāda-vaṇṇanā

The view that "the self and the world arise without a cause" is called Adhiccasamuppanna. Those who hold that view are called Adhiccasamuppannikas. Adhiccasamuppanna means arising without a cause.

68-73. Asaññasatta is the pinnacle of the teaching; it means an individual existence (attabhāva) consisting only of form (rūpa) without the arising of consciousness. The arising of those non-percipient beings should be understood thus: a certain person, having gone forth in a non-Buddhist sect, performs the preliminary work on the air-kasina (vāyokasiṇa) and produces the fourth jhāna. Upon emerging from the jhāna, he sees the fault in consciousness, thinking that if there is consciousness...
109:
...suffering and all dangers such as having one's hands cut off occur only because of the existence of consciousness. "Enough with this consciousness; the state of being without consciousness is alone peaceful." Thus, seeing the fault in consciousness, a person with undiminished jhāna, when he dies, is reborn among the non-percipient beings (asaññasatta). His consciousness ceases right here in this five-constituent realm (pañcavokāra-bhava) with the cessation of the death-consciousness, and only the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) becomes manifest there.

Those non-percipient brahmās remain there—just as an arrow shot by the force of a bowstring travels in the sky only as long as the force of the bowstring lasts—similarly, those beings who have arisen being propelled by the force of jhāna remain for only as long as the force of jhāna lasts. When the force of jhāna is exhausted, the aggregate of form disappears in that realm, and the rebirth-perception (consciousness) arises here in this sense-sphere. Because their falling from that non-percipient realm is made manifest by that perception which has arisen here, it is said: "With the arising of perception, those deities fall from that body." Santatāya means because of being manifest. The rest of the sequence of words is plain. The Takkīvāda (doctrine based on reasoning) should also be understood in the same manner as already stated.

## Aparantakappikavaṇṇanā

Having thus shown the eighteen Speculators about the Past (Pubbantakappika), the Buddha now said, "There are, bhikkhus," etc., to show the forty-four Speculators about the Future (Aparantakappika). In that passage, they are called Aparantakappikas because they speculate and grasp the future, which is called the 'aparanta' (the end part). Or, they are called Aparantakappikas because they have speculations about the future. Thus, the rest of the sequence of words should be understood in the same manner as previously stated.

## Saññīvāda-vaṇṇanā

In the term uddhamāghātanikā, death is called āghātana. They are called Uddhamāghātanikas because they speak of the self as existing in the later period above (after) death. The doctrine that "there is perception" is called Saññīvāda; those who hold that doctrine are called Saññīvādās.

76-77. In the passages such as rūpī attā, they designate that "the self has form, and after death it is healthy (permanent) and percipient," either by taking the kasina-form as the "self" and the perception occurring in that kasina-form as the "perception of the self," or by mere reasoning like the Ājīvikas and others. In that context, arogā (healthy) means permanent (nicca). However, they designate that "the self is formless, and after death it is healthy and percipient," either by taking the sign of the formless attainment as the "self" and the perception in that attainment as the "perception of the self," or by mere reasoning like the Nigaṇṭhas and others. The third view is a view that proceeds by way of grasping a mixture (both form and formless). The fourth view proceeds by mere reasoning alone.
110:
The second tetrad should be understood in the same way as stated in the Antānantika view. In the third tetrad, it should be understood as: one percipient of unity (ekattasaññī) by virtue of one who has attained meditative absorption; one percipient of diversity (nānattasaññī) by virtue of one who has not attained absorption; one percipient of the limited (parittasaññī) by virtue of a limited kasiṇa; and one percipient of the immeasurable (appamāṇasaññī) by virtue of an expansive kasiṇa. In the fourth tetrad, however, seeing a being arising in the planes of the third and fourth jhānas with the divine eye, one takes the view: "The self is purely happy." Seeing a being arising in hell, one takes the view: "The self is purely miserable." Seeing a being arising among humans, one takes the view: "The self is both happy and miserable." Seeing a being arising in the Vehapphala Brahma realm, one takes the view: "The self has feeling that is neither-miserable-nor-happy." Specifically, those who have attained the knowledge of recollecting past lives are speculators on the past (pubbantakappika), and those with the divine eye are speculators on the future (aparantakappika).

## Commentary on the Doctrine of Non-perception (Asaññīvāda)

78-83. The doctrine of non-perception should be understood by virtue of the two tetrads mentioned at the beginning of the doctrine of perception (saññīvāda). The doctrine of neither-perception-nor-non-perception should be understood in the same way. Indeed, in that doctrine of perception, those are the views of those who hold "the self is percipient," whereas here in the doctrine of non-perception and the doctrine of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, they hold "the self is non-percipient" and "the self is neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient." In holding such views, there is no need to search for a specific reason. It has been said that the grasp of one with wrong views is like a madman's basket.

## Commentary on the Doctrine of Annihilationism (Ucchedavāda)

In the doctrine of annihilationism, "sato" means of an existing (being). "Uccheda" means cutting off; "vināsa" means disappearance; "vibhava" means the passing away of the nature of being. All these are synonyms for one another. In that doctrine of annihilationism, two types of persons—those who have attained the divine eye and those who have not—hold the view of annihilation. One who has attained the higher knowledge, seeing the passing away (cuti) [of an Arahant] with the divine eye but not seeing the rebirth, or because they are only able to see the passing away and not the rebirth, holds the view of annihilation. One who has not attained the higher knowledge holds the view of annihilation either by thinking, "Who can know the world beyond?" or through greed for sensual pleasures, or through reasoning (takka) such as, "Just as leaves fallen from a tree do not grow again, so it is with beings." Here, it should be understood that these seven views arise by differentiating in this way and that through the power of craving and wrong views.

In that Pali, "rūpī" means having form. "Cātumahābhūtika" means consisting of the four great elements. "This thing of the parents" means what is born from the parents. What is that? It is the semen and blood.
111:
Because it is well-produced and born from the semen and blood which are the property of the parents, it is called "mātāpettikasambhava" (the self born of parents). Thus, emphasizing the physical body, one speaks of the human existence as "the self." "Ittheke" means "thus some" (hold this view).

The second teacher rejects that view and speaks of a divine self. "Dibba" means one born in the heavenly world. "Kāmāvacara" means one belonging to the six heavens of the sense sphere. Because of eating food made into morsels, it is called "kabaḷīkārāhārabhakkha" (one who eats solid food).

"Manomaya" means one produced by the mind of jhāna. "Sabbanga-paccangī" means one complete with all major and minor limbs. "Ahīnindriya" means one with unimpaired faculties. This is stated by virtue of the faculties that exist in the Brahma world and by virtue of the shape of the remaining faculties.

88-92. The meaning of the terms beginning with "sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ samatikkamā" has been stated in the Visuddhimagga. In the terms beginning with "ākāsānañcāyatanūpago," however, the meaning should be understood as one who has reached the state of the sphere of infinite space. In this doctrine of annihilationism, the remaining collection of words is clear.

## Commentary on the Doctrine of Nibbāna in the Present Life

In the doctrine of Nibbāna in the present life, "diṭṭhadhamma" refers to the nature evident to the senses; it is a designation for the self-attainment obtained in various planes of existence. The occurrence of Nibbāna in the self-attainment evident to the senses is called "diṭṭhadhammanibbāna"; it means the subsiding of suffering in this very self-attainment. Those who speak thus are called "diṭṭhadhammanibbānavādā" (those who speak of Nibbāna in the present life). "Paramadiṭṭhadhammanibbāna" means the supreme, or especially excellent, Nibbāna in the present life.

"Pañcahi kāmaguṇehi" means by the five strands of sensual pleasure such as pleasant forms, etc., or by the five fetters. "Samappito" means being well-fixed or attached. "Samangībhūto" means being endowed with. "Paricāreti" means directing the faculties as one pleases among those strands of sensual pleasure, making them wander, or bringing them here and there. Or it means enjoying, delighting, or playing. Here, there are two kinds of strands of sensual pleasure: human and divine. Human strands of sensual pleasure should be understood as similar to those of King Mandhātu; divine strands of sensual pleasure should be understood as similar to those of the divine king of the Paranimmita-vasavatti heaven. For those who have reached such sensual pleasures, they designate the attainment of Nibbāna in the present life.
112:
In the second turn (vāra), they should be understood as impermanent (anicca) in the sense of non-existence after having come to be; as suffering (dukkha) in the sense of oppression; and as subject to change (vipariṇāmadhamma) in the sense of abandoning their natural state. Because of that change, which is called the transformation of those sense pleasures, sorrow (soka), lamentation (parideva), pain (dukkha), grief (domanassa), and despair (upāyāsa) arise in the manner stated: "What I once had, I no longer have."

In that context, sorrow (soka) has the characteristic of inner burning. Lamentation (parideva) has the characteristic of wailing based on that sorrow. Pain (dukkha) has the characteristic of bodily oppression. Grief (domanassa) has the characteristic of mental affliction. Despair (upāyāsa) has the characteristic of mental dejection. The meaning of the words beginning with "quite secluded from sense pleasures" has been stated in the Visuddhimagga. 

'Vitakkita' refers to initial thought (vitakka) which occurs by way of directing the mind onto the object. 'Vicārita' refers to sustained thought (vicāra) which occurs by way of continued stroking of the object. Because it is associated with this vitakka and vicāra, this first jhāna appears coarse and as if having thorns.

97-98. 'Pītigata' is simply joy (pīti). 'Cetaso uppilāvitatta' is that which causes the state of the mind's upliftment (pīti). 'Cetaso ābhoga' is the repeated directing of the mind, attention, and advertence towards that happiness (sukha) after emerging from jhāna. The remaining meanings in this 'doctrine of Nibbāna in the present life' (diṭṭhadhammanibbānavāda) are clear.

By this much, all sixty-two views have been explained. Among those views, only seven are annihilationist views (ucchedadiṭṭhi); the remaining views are eternalist views (sassatadiṭṭhi).

100-104. Now, with the turn (vāra) beginning with "Monks, by these things...", He concludes all those speculators about the future (aparantakappika) together and reveals His omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa). Again, with the turn beginning with "Monks, by these things...", He concludes all those speculators about the past and the future (pubbantāparantakappika) together and reveals that same omniscience. Thus, even when asking, "Monks, what are those things?", He asks only about His omniscience; and when answering, He reveals only His omniscience, having extracted the sixty-two views as if weighing the dispositions (ajjhāsaya) of beings with a scale, or as if extracting sand from the foot of Mount Sineru. Thus, this teaching has come by way of connection (anusandhi).

There are three types of connections in a Sutta: connection by question (pucchānusandhi), connection by disposition (ajjhāsayānusandhi), and connection by sequence (yathānusandhi). Among these, when it was said, another monk said this to the Blessed One: "What..."
113:
"Venerable Sir, what is the near shore? What is the far shore? What is sinking in the middle? What is grounding on a sandbank? What is being caught by humans? What is being caught by non-humans? What is being caught by a whirlpool? What is internal rottenness?" (Saṃ. Ni. 4.241). The connection by question (pucchānusandhi) should be understood by way of the Sutta answered by the Blessed One to those asking in this manner.

Then, a reflection arose in the mind of a certain monk: "So it seems, friends, form is non-self... feeling... perception... formations... consciousness is non-self. What self will the deeds done by the non-self touch?" Then the Blessed One, knowing the reflection in that monk's mind with His own mind, addressed the monks: "Monks, it is possible that some hollow man here, being ignorant and fallen into nescience, with a mind dominated by craving, might think he should overstep the Teacher's instruction thus: 'So it seems, friends, form is non-self... [as above] ...will they touch?' Monks, what do you think? Is form permanent or impermanent?" (Ma. Ni. 3.10). Thus, the connection by disposition (ajjhāsayānusandhi) should be understood by way of the Sutta spoken by the Blessed One after knowing the desires and dispositions of others.

In those Suttas where the teaching proceeds further by way of a doctrine that is either suitable to or opposite to the doctrine with which the teaching began at the start, the connection by sequence (yathānusandhi) should be understood by way of those. For example: in the Ākaṅkheyya Sutta, the teaching begins with virtue (sīla) in the lower part, and the six super-knowledges (abhiññā) come in the upper part. In the Vattha Sutta, the teaching begins with defilements (kilesa) in the lower part, and the divine abodes (brahmavihāra) come in the upper part. In the Kosambaka Sutta, it begins with quarreling in the lower part, and the principles of cordiality (sāraṇīyadhamma) come in the upper part. In the Kakacūpama Sutta, it begins with intolerance in the lower part, and the simile of the saw comes in the upper part. In this Brahmajāla Sutta also, the teaching begins by way of views (diṭṭhi) in the lower part, and the explanation of emptiness (suññatā) comes in the upper part. Therefore, it is said: "Thus, this teaching has come by way of connection by sequence (yathānusandhi)."

## Commentary on the Section on Agitation and Vacillation

105-117. Now, for the purpose of showing the division of boundaries, the teaching beginning with "Therein, monks..." is commenced. That teaching also [shows] that the experience of those venerable recluses and brahmins who do not know and do not see, and who are possessed by craving, is merely the agitation and vacillation of craving by which...
114:
Those recluses and brahmins, being joyful through the enjoyment of views, the pleasure of views, and the experience of views, proclaim the self and the world to be eternal based on four grounds. For those venerable recluses and brahmins who thus proclaim, not knowing and not seeing the nature of things as they really are, their experience (vedanā) is merely the arrival of craving for those who are possessed by craving. That experience is indeed only the agitation and vacillation of one who is anxious through craving and views. This agitation and vacillation through what is called view and what is called craving is like a stake driven into a heap of chaff; it is not stable and steady like the vision of a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna). This method applies also to the partial-eternalists and so forth.

## Explanation of the Section on the Condition of Contact

118-130. Again, the Buddha began the teaching with "Therein, bhikkhus, those recluses and brahmins who are eternalists..." and so forth, in order to show the sequence of conditions. Therein, by the words "that too is conditioned by contact," he shows that the experience agitated by craving and views—whereby they proclaim the self and the world to be eternal based on four grounds while being joyful through the enjoyment of views, the pleasure of views, and the experience of views—is also conditioned by contact. This method is the same in all cases.

131-143. Now, to show the powerful nature of contact as a condition for the experience of views, he said again: "Therein, bhikkhus, those recluses and brahmins who are eternalists..." and so forth. Therein, "they [cannot experience] apart from contact" means there is no possibility that those recluses and brahmins would experience that feeling without contact. For example, just as a pillar is a powerful condition for supporting a house that is about to fall, and that house cannot stand without the support of the pillar, so too contact is a powerful condition for feeling; he shows that without contact, this experience of views cannot exist. This method is the same in all cases.

## Explanation of the Discourse on the Cycle of Existence as the Basis for Those Following Views

Now, by the method starting with "Therein, bhikkhus, those recluses and brahmins who are eternalists and proclaim the self and the world to be eternal based on four grounds," he summarizes all experiences of views with "those recluses and brahmins who are partial-eternalists," and so forth. Why? For the purpose of including them under contact further on. How? By saying, "All of them experience by repeatedly touching with the six bases of contact." Therein, the six bases of contact are: the eye-contact base, the ear-contact base, the nose-contact base, the tongue-contact base, the body-contact base, and the mind-contact base. In the senses of origin, meeting place, cause, and mere designation...
115:
This word 'āyatana' occurs [in various senses]. Among those senses, in the passage "Kamboja is the āyatana of horses, the Southern Path (Dakkhiṇāpatha) is the āyatana of cattle," it occurs in the sense of origin (sañjāti), meaning the place of birth. In the passage "Birds resort to that āyatana which is delightful to the mind," it occurs in the sense of a meeting place (samosaraṇa). In the passage "When there is a cause (āyatana), there is [the result]," it occurs in the sense of cause (kāraṇa). In the passage "They dwell in leaf-huts in the forest-base (araññāyatana)," it occurs in the sense of mere designation (paṇṇattimatta). This word āyatana is suitable in all three senses—origin and so forth—in this context [of the bases of contact]. For in the eye and so forth, the states beginning with contact as the fifth arise and meet; and those [bases] are the cause of those states; therefore, they are called āyatanas.

In this context, however, by the method "Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact," the teaching is presented with contact as the head. Starting with contact, the sequence of conditions is shown, and thus "bases of contact" and so forth are spoken.

"They experience by repeatedly touching" (phussa phussa paṭisaṃvedenti) means they experience after having touched again and again. Here, although it is spoken as if the bases have the function of touching, it should not be understood that they have the function of touching. For the bases do not touch; only contact touches the respective objects. The bases are shown by being included within contact. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood thus: all those recluses and brahmins, through contact produced by the six bases of contact, touch objects such as forms and experience the feeling that is the cause of those views.

In the passages such as "With feeling as condition, craving [arises]," feeling refers to the feeling produced by the six bases of contact. That feeling is a condition for craving—divided into craving for forms and so forth—by way of the proximity (decisive support) condition (upanissaya). Therefore, it is said: "With feeling as condition, craving [arises]." That craving is a condition for the four types of clinging by way of both the proximity condition and the conascence condition (sahajāta). Likewise, clinging is a condition for existence, and existence is a condition for birth by way of the proximity condition.

Here, "birth" (jāti) should be understood as the five aggregates along with their transformations. Birth is a condition for aging and death, as well as for sorrow and so forth, by way of the proximity condition. This is a summary here; the detailed explanation of Dependent Origination is stated in the Visuddhimagga. Here, only what is necessary for this [Brahmajāla Sutta] should be understood. For when the Blessed One speaks the discourse on the cycle of existence, [he says]: "Bhikkhus, the preceding point of ignorance is not evident, such that one could say, 'Before this, ignorance did not exist, but afterwards it came to be.' Yet, bhikkhus, it is said thus, and it is evident that 'Ignorance is conditioned by this.'" Thus, either with ignorance as the head, or [as he says], "Bhikkhus, the preceding..."
116:
The prior limit of craving for existence is not evident... 'Because of this cause, craving for existence arises'—thus He taught, making craving the head. Or, 'Monks, the prior limit of the view of existence is not evident... Because of this cause, the view of existence arises'—thus He taught, making wrong view the head. However, in this Brahmajāla Sutta, while teaching with wrong view as the head, He taught the wrong views that arise due to attachment to feeling, and then He taught the dependent origination rooted in feeling. By teaching thus, He showed that those with such wrong views, holding onto this view, wander and circulate from this existence to that, and from that existence to this, within the three realms, the four modes of birth, the five destinations, the seven stations of consciousness, and the nine abodes of beings. Like an ox yoked to a mill, like a dog bound to a post, or like a boat wrecked by the wind, they merely revolve within the suffering of the cycle and are unable to lift their heads above the suffering of the cycle.

## Explanation of the Discourse on the Cessation of the Cycle, etc.

Having thus taught the cycle (vaṭṭa) which is the standing place of those with wrong views, He now spoke the words beginning with, 'Monks, when a monk...' desiring to show the cessation of the cycle (vivaṭṭa) by making the monk who practices meditation the standing place. Therein, 'yato' means 'when'. 'Of the six bases of contact' refers to those same six bases of contact by which those with wrong views, through contacting and experiencing, continue to revolve in the cycle. Regarding the terms such as 'arising' (samudaya), the arising and so forth of the bases of contact should be understood according to the method already mentioned in the meditation on feeling (vedanākammaṭṭhāna), such as 'with the arising of ignorance, the eye arises'. However, unlike what was said in that meditation on feeling as 'with the arising of contact, with the cessation of contact', here, in the case of the eye and so forth, it should be understood as 'with the arising of nutriment, with the cessation of nutriment'. In the case of the mind base (manāyatana), it should be understood as 'with the arising of name-and-form, with the cessation of name-and-form'.

'He knows further' means that a person with wrong view knows only the wrong view. This monk, however, knows the wrong view and also knows that which is further than the wrong view—virtue, concentration, wisdom, and liberation—up until Arahatship. Who knows in this way? An Arahat knows, a Non-returner, a Once-returner, a Stream-enterer, a monk who is learned and a bearer of the scriptures knows, and a person who has begun insight meditation (vipassanā) knows. This teaching, however, is concluded at the summit of Arahatship.
117:
Having thus taught the cessation of the cycle (vivaṭṭa), He began again, saying, 'Monks, those who...' in order to show that 'there is no one with wrong views who escapes from the net of the teaching.' In that passage, 'antojālီkatā' means they are made to be within this net of my teaching (they are included). 'Ettha sitā vā' means they are dependent on, clinging to, or remaining within this net of my teaching. 'Ummuzzamānā ummuzzanti' (emerging, they emerge)—what does this mean? Whether those with wrong views sink down or rise up, they do so while being dependent on the net of my teaching. Being included in this net of the teaching, connected to this net, and remaining within the net, they emerge. There is no one with wrong views who is not included in this teaching.

'Sukhuma-acchikena' means with a net that has subtle and small meshes (holes). The Blessed One is like a fisherman; the teaching is like a net; the ten-thousandfold world system is like a small amount of water; the sixty-two types of wrong views are like large creatures such as fish and turtles. Just as a fisherman standing on the shore sees the large creatures caught within the net, the Blessed One sees all those with wrong views included within the net of His teaching. Thus should the comparison with the simile be understood.

Having thus shown how all those with wrong views are included in this net of the teaching because all views are encompassed by these sixty-two views, He now spoke the words beginning with, 'Monks, the body of the Tathāgata has the cord of existence cut,' desiring to show that He Himself is not included in any existence or mode of birth. In that passage, 'netti' is so called because one is led or pulled by it. It is a name for a rope that pulls after being tied to the neck. Here, however, craving for existence is intended as 'netti' because it is like a rope. That craving is called 'bhavanetti' (the cord of existence) because it ties the multitude of beings by the neck and leads them to various existences. He is called 'ucchinnabhavanettika' because He has the cord of existence cut by the weapon of the path of Arahatship.

'After the breaking up of the body' means after death. 'With the exhaustion of life' means because the life-faculty is entirely exhausted and finished, or it means the state of not taking rebirth again. 'They will not see Him' means that neither gods nor humans will see that Tathāgata; it means He will reach a state that cannot be designated (apaṇṇattikabhāva).
118:
"Bhikkhus, for example," in this statement, the comparison is as follows: The body of the Tathāgata is like a mango tree; the craving that occurred in previous lives, depending on which this body exists, is like the large stalk produced on the tree. Just as a cluster of mangoes—numbering five, twelve, or eighteen—is attached to that stalk, so too, when there is craving, being bound by craving, the five aggregates, twelve bases, and eighteen elements that will arise in the future (are attached to that stalk of craving). When that stalk is cut, all those mangoes follow the fate of the stalk; that is to say, they are cut off because the stalk is cut. In the same way, as long as the stalk of craving for existence (bhavanetti) is not yet cut, the five aggregates, twelve bases, and eighteen elements that would arise in the future follow the course of that craving for existence; when that craving for existence is cut, all those phenomena are indeed cut off. 

Just as on that very tree, due to the touch of the venom of a frog-thorn, it gradually withers and dies, and there remains only the mere expression, "In this place, there used to be such a tree," but no one can see that tree anymore; in the same way, due to the touch of the Noble Path, the sap of craving is exhausted, and like something that has gradually withered, when this body breaks up, after the breaking up of the body and the exhaustion of the life-faculty, gods and humans will no longer see the Tathāgata. There will only be the mere expression, "Such was the teaching of a Teacher of such a nature." Thus, the Buddha concluded the discourse, leading it to the Nibbāna element without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbāna-dhātu).

When the Blessed One had spoken this discourse, the Venerable Ānanda, having reflected on the entire sutta from beginning to end, thought: "The Blessed One has preached this sutta demonstrating the power of the Buddha's knowledge, but he has not yet given a name to the sutta. Now, I shall ask him to give it a name." Thinking thus, he addressed the Blessed One.

In the words beginning with "Tasmātiha tvaṃ" (Therefore, you...), the connection of the meaning is: "Ānanda, because in this Dhamma-discourse (Dhamma-pariyāya), the benefit of this life and the benefit of the future life are distinguished, therefore, you should remember this Dhamma-discourse as the 'Net of Advantage' (Atthajāla). Because many doctrines (Dhamma) are preached in this sutta, you should also remember it as the 'Net of Dhamma' (Dhammajāla). Because the supreme Omniscient Knowledge is distinguished here in its noble sense, you should also remember it as the 'Net of the Supreme' (Brahmajāla). Because the sixty-two wrong views are distinguished here, you should also remember it as the 'Net of Views' (Diṭṭhijāla). Because, having heard this Dhamma-discourse, even the Māra of the gods (Devaputta-māra), the Māra of the aggregates (Khandha-māra), and the Māra of death (Maccu-māra)..."
119:
"...and even the Māra of defilements (Kilesa-māra) can be subdued, therefore, you should also remember it as the 'Incomparable Victory in Battle' (Anuttara Saṅgāmavijaya)."

"The Blessed One said this" means the entire sutta from the end of the introduction (nidāna) to the end where it says, "You should also remember it as the Incomparable Victory in Battle." The Blessed One spoke, revealing the extremely profound Omniscient Knowledge, which has a foundation unattainable by the wisdom of others, destroying the great darkness of wrong views just as the sun dispels the darkness.

"Those bhikkhus were delighted" means those bhikkhus were satisfied in their own minds; it means they had uplifted minds due to the joy directed towards the Buddha. "The words spoken by the Blessed One" refers to the words of the Blessed One who was speaking with a Brahma-voice (brahmassara), which is pleasant and agreeable to the ear like the song of the Karavīka bird, and which is like a sprinkling of nectar upon the hearts of wise people—this sutta being endowed with such a variety of methods and beauty of teaching. "They rejoiced (abhinanduṃ)" means they both rejoiced repeatedly and accepted it. This word "abhinanda" appears in the sense of craving in passages such as "abhinandati abhivadati" (he rejoices and welcomes). It appears in the sense of approaching (upagamana) in passages such as "Both gods and humans approach (abhinandanti) only food."

"When a man who has been long absent returns safely from afar,
his kinsmen, friends, and well-wishers rejoice (abhinandanti) at his arrival."

In such passages, it appears in the sense of accepting (sampaṭicchana). In passages such as "having rejoiced and appreciated (abhinanditvā anumoditvā)," it appears in the sense of repeated rejoicing (anumodana). Here, it is appropriate in the senses of both repeated rejoicing and accepting. Therefore, it is said: "'They rejoiced' means they both rejoiced repeatedly and accepted it."

The bhikkhus, appreciating the well-spoken words
of the One of such a nature (Tādi), who is unshaken by the eight worldly conditions,
accepted them with their heads bowed,
saying, "Sādhu, Sādhu."

"In this exposition (veyyākaraṇa)" means in this sutta which is without verses. Because it is without verses, this sutta is called an exposition (veyyākaraṇa).

"The ten thousandfold world system" means the world system with the extent of ten thousand universes (cakkavāḷa). "It shook" means it should be understood that it did not shake only at the conclusion of the sutta. It is said, "while it was being spoken." Therefore, while the sixty-two wrong views were being dismantled...
120:
It should be understood that the earth shook sixty-two times at the conclusion of each of those specific views as they were being taught.
